analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal estate tax rates and raises the estate tax exemption to $2 million.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan-by-Democrat-standards estate tax cut with 100 House sponsors died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut federal estate tax rates by up to 20% and gradually raised the amount of an estate shielded from the tax, reaching $2 million by 2009 with inflation adjustments after that. It also made it easier for heirs of closely held family businesses to spread out estate tax payments, and swapped a federal credit for state death taxes for a smaller deduction. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to large estates and owners of closely held family businesses. The federal estate tax in 2000 applied only to estates above roughly $675,000, so the bill's benefits would have gone overwhelmingly to families with substantial wealth — the bill itself sets the new exemption at $1.3 million in 2001, rising to $2 million by 2009 [S3]. Family business owners gained from both the rate cuts and the eased payment-extension rules [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Heirs to large estates and family businesses

how_it_helps.text: Reduces every estate tax bracket by 20%, lowering the top rate from 55% to 44%, and to 39.6% for amounts over $2.5 million after 2009 [S3].
Raises the exemption equivalent of the unified credit from $675,000 to $1.3 million in 2001-2002, stepping up to $2 million by 2009, with cost-of-living adjustments after 2010 [S3].
Repeals the complicated family-owned business deduction and replaces it with the simpler, broader exemption and rate cuts [S3].
Raises the number of partners or shareholders a closely held business may have — from 15 to 45 — while still qualifying heirs to stretch estate tax payments over many years [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, through the lost estate and gift tax revenue, which must be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing. State governments also lose: the bill repeals the federal credit that returned state death taxes to federal taxpayers' benefit and replaces it with a mere deduction, meaning estates pay both federal and state taxes with only partial offset [S3].

drawbacks.text: The tax cut would reduce federal revenue, since the estate and gift tax was a meaningful revenue source applied only to the largest estates; other taxpayers would eventually bear the difference [S3].
Repealing the credit for state death taxes converts it to a deduction, which would cost state governments revenue on large estates and could pressure states to rewrite their own estate taxes [S2].

The bill does not repeal the estate tax, so the largest estates above $2 million would still face substantial tax and families would continue to bear the costs of estate planning and administration [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a real tax cut, but its design channels it to a narrow group: only estates above roughly $1.3 million would benefit, meaning the gains concentrate among the wealthiest families and business owners while the revenue loss spreads across all federal taxpayers. It simplifies the code by replacing the family-business deduction with broader exemptions, a genuine efficiency gain, but the state-credit repeal shifts costs onto state governments. Weighing it honestly, this is a targeted tax cut for concentrated wealth more than broad relief.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tanner (D-TN) introduced the bill on September 27, 2000, with 25 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
99 Democrats had signed on as cosponsors by the end of the Congress [S4].
No further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill never received a hearing or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died quietly, the existing estate tax stayed in place with no revenue loss; the estate-planning and wealth-management industry avoided the disruption of a major rewrite, and state governments kept the federal credit arrangement for the time being.

for.name: John Tanner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 25 original Democratic cosponsors on day one.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — the bill was a moderate Democratic alternative in the 2000 estate tax debate — but the record shows no one publicly opposing it; it simply died in committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Heirs to large estates and wealthy families
industries.note: The bill's exemptions and rate cuts would flow almost entirely to estates above $1.3 million — roughly the wealthiest few percent of decedents — while the revenue loss spreads across all federal taxpayers. Because the bill died, this group gained nothing.

Rate cuts, a higher exemption, and a widened payment-extension rule (45 instead of 15 partners or shareholders) would have eased estate tax burdens on closely held businesses. Its interest runs against ordinary taxpayers, who fund the revenue loss.
Repealing the federal credit for state death taxes and replacing it with a deduction would have reduced the effective offset estates receive for state taxes, costing states revenue on large estates.

industries.industry: Estate planning, tax, and wealth-management professionals
industries.note: Lower rates and a bigger exemption would reduce demand for estate planning, but the tax's survival at lower rates would have kept the planning industry in business. The bill's failure left the status quo — and the industry's market — fully intact.
